title: Calling the weapons back
hookLine: a young man with the gods' weapons asks the one question that matters next
carry: the wise know samhara, the calling back
last: THE GURU GIVES MANTRAS TO THE READY.

lines: THE USUAL QUESTION: WHAT CAN IT DO?
cards: Hand someone the keys to something enormous and listen to their first question. A new driver with a fast car. A new manager with the power to fire people.
An eighteen-year-old with a credit card. It's nearly always: what can this do? How fast, how far, how much?
Rama has just been handed the weapons of the gods. And walking on through the forest, he asks Vishvamitra something quieter, and wiser.

teach.h: TEACH ME TO CALL THEM BACK.
teach.b: I've received the weapons, Rama says, and even the gods would find them hard to overcome. Now teach me how to call them back.
In Sanskrit, the release is prayoga; the withdrawal is samhara. Vishvamitra is delighted, and teaches him. Again the powers appear, a new company of shining beings, palms joined.
These are the withdrawals: the knowledge of how to stop what you've started. Why does Valmiki give this a whole moment? Because in the epics a weapon you can't call back is a disaster.
Rama, this young, asks for the brake before he ever touches the accelerator.

teach.h: THE GITA: YADĀ SAṂHARATE CĀYAṂ KŪRMO 'ṄGĀNĪVA SARVAŚAḤ.
teach.b: And the same word comes back in the Bhagavad Gita.
Krishna describes a person of steady wisdom as someone who can draw the senses back from what pulls at them, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs: yada samharate, when he withdraws. Samhara, again.
That's a Hindu idea of strength. Not only what you can unleash, but what you can call back: a word, an appetite, a temper. The road goes on to a green hermitage on a hill, with deer grazing.
This is Siddhashrama, the sage says, where Vishnu once did his austerities, the hermitage of Vamana, who asked King Bali for three steps of land and crossed the worlds in three strides.
My sacrifice is waiting here. And here the weapons will be needed.

how: Traditional teachers often point to Rama's request for the withdrawals of the weapons as a sign of his character, and the Gita's image of the tortoise drawing in its limbs uses the same word for self-mastery.

o: powers Rama learns both to release and to call back
a gift Rama refuses until he has proved himself
the spoils Rama takes from Tataka's empty forest

games.q: release and return — tap the pairs.
p: draws in its limbs, like the wise

s: Rama asks how far the weapons can reach
he asks how to call them back.
the withdrawals also appear as shining beings
a second company, palms joined, at Rama's service.
in the Gita, a wise person is one who can withdraw the senses, like a tortoise its limbs
and the Gita's word for it, samharate, is the same root as Rama's samhara.

games.q: you're Rama. you've just received the weapons of the gods. what do you ask the sage?
o: how do I call them back?
games.why: he asks for the samhara, the withdrawals. the sage, delighted, teaches him. the Gita later uses the same word for the wise drawing in their senses.

practice: Sit like the Gita's tortoise. Let attention come in from the world one sense at a time: the eyes soften, then the ears, then the busy hands go still. Every breath has a release and a return.
Then think of one thing you set loose today, a mood, a comment, a scroll that ran too long, and practice calling it back, the way a breath comes home. If you pray, ask for that kind of strength.

wordCard.voice: The weapons. Rama asks not only how to release them but how to withdraw them, and Vishvamitra teaches him the samhara, the calling back.

orig.note: Sanskrit saṃhāra: drawing back, withdrawal; here, the power to call a weapon back.

carryVoice: Your line: the wise know samhara, the calling back. Rama asked for the brake first. See you tomorrow.
